thread.title: Cash Neutral Means What? My understanding of the term based

author: Mark Bern, CFA
title: Cash Neutral Means What? My understanding of the term based
text:
Cash Neutral Means What? 
My understanding of the term based upon what little Apple ( AAPL ) CFO, Luca Maestri , said stated earlier this month is that the company intends to keep enough cash on its balance sheet needed for operations, dividends, R&D efforts, and planned acquisitions along with a buffer to handle unforeseen contingencies. The rest the company plans on returning to shareholders over time. 
Or, it could mean that it plans of giving it cash hoard back to shareholders over a pre-determined period of time while operating on the cash it generates from operations. 
The difference is that in the second scenario the company will likely continue to build up another cash hoard over time because it just cannot find uses for all the cash it generates. But that is not really cash neutral in my mind unless management is planning to increase its acquisitions efforts to buy more companies with potentially faster growth prospects. That would probably end up generating even more cash, though, so what would management do with that? That is the sort of problem every CEO wants. 
The thing is that no matter how we slice or define the term it means that Apple can do so many things that other companies can only dream about. That leads us to the true beauty of Apple’s situation: 
Flexible Cash Structure 
Never in the history of mankind has any company had so much flexibility in its capital structure. Apple could buy just about anything it wanted. Why? Because it has so much cash. The company has an estimated $285 billion in cash. It could buy any company in the U.S. outside of the 15 largest companies by market capitalization for cash at current valuations. Each year with the excess cash it generates it could buy almost any company outside of the top 100 in the U.S., again for cash, because it generates so much free cash flow. Of course, it probably will not make such moves because eventually it would run into antitrust issues and it is unlikely that management would want to stray too far from its core competencies.
